issues.legal_issue: A restricted lifetime interest in property created for a Hindu woman by a will or other instrument does not become absolute ownership under the general rule for female Hindu property.
material_facts: The property owner’s 1944 will gave his daughter the right to reside in a house and receive its rental income during her lifetime.
The will prohibited her from alienating, mortgaging, gifting, selling, or transferring the house, and provided that her brother would be its owner subject to her rights.
The daughter claimed that the interest became absolute ownership under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
issues.conclusion: The interest remained limited to the daughter’s lifetime and did not become absolute ownership.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, generally makes property possessed by a female Hindu her full property, but Section 14(2) excepts property acquired under a will, gift, or other instrument that prescribes a restricted estate. Reading Section 14(1) to enlarge an expressly restricted testamentary interest would make Section 14(2) and Section 30 otiose. The Court relied on Mst. Karmi v. Amru, AIR 1971 SC 745; Navneet Lal @ Rangi v. Gokul, AIR 1976 SC 794; Jagan Singh (Dead) Through LRs. v. Dhanwanti, (2012) 2 SCC 628; and Sadhu Singh v. Gurdwara Sahib Narike, AIR 2006 SC 3282. It distinguished Balwant Kaur v. Chanan Singh, AIR 2000 SC 1908, where the will, read as a whole, gave only a limited estate.

rule.if: female_property_claim and interest_created_by_instrument and instrument_limits_interest_to_lifetime and claim_to_expand_interest

predicates.female_property_claim: A female heir claims ownership of property.
predicates.interest_created_by_instrument: The property owner gives the female heir an interest in the property through a will, gift, or other instrument.
predicates.instrument_limits_interest_to_lifetime: The instrument limits the female heir’s interest to her lifetime.
predicates.claim_to_expand_interest: The female heir claims that the restricted interest should become full ownership.

issues.definition: When a female heir claims expanded ownership of property given to her by an instrument that limits her interest to her lifetime, the limited interest remains limited.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that a person was destitute cannot be considered as a factual basis for expanding a property interest when no factual foundation for that claim was laid before the lower courts.
material_facts: The appellant argued that her father had created the life interest because she was destitute.
No factual foundation for her alleged destitution had been laid before the lower courts.
The Court treated whether a person is destitute as a question of fact and did not consider the issue further.
issues.conclusion: The Court did not consider the destitution-based contention because it lacked a factual foundation in the lower courts.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a person is destitute is a question of fact. The Court noted that the term was not defined in the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, or the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and described its ordinary meaning as being without resources or necessities; it also referred to a person having no support, no settled abode, and no visible means of subsistence. Because no factual foundation had been laid below, the Court held that the issue did not require consideration.

predicates.appeal_on_lower_court_record: A party appeals from a decision made on the record before the lower courts.
predicates.destitution_claim_raised: A party asserts that a person was destitute.
predicates.no_factual_foundation_below: The party asserting destitution did not lay a factual foundation for that assertion before the lower courts.

issues.definition: In an appeal on the lower-court record, a destitution claim is not considered when it was raised without a factual foundation below.
